statement: Week 5, day 2 continues the discussion on storage engines; the agenda is two problem statements that build foundational concepts and building blocks for building interesting systems or getting the maximum out of existing systems.
detail: The board agenda lists the two problems: a word dictionary without any DB, and a super fast KV store.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Week 5, day 2nd and we'll continue our discussion on storage engines.

statement: Both systems discussed today are actively used in production to a huge extent; they are not just theoretical.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And both of them are actively used in production. It's not something that's just theoretical.

statement: Problem statement: build a word dictionary without using any traditional database (no MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Memcache, nothing); you have to be creative.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What we will do is we will build a word dictionary without using any traditional database.

statement: The dictionary needs to be 'quote-unquote' scalable on both sides, storage and API servers, though some constraints will obviously exist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This thing needs to be scalable, which means you should not be worrying about scale, but then obviously some constraints would be there

statement: Typically any system design can be bifurcated into two parts: storage and compute. Compute is basically the API servers and storage means the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So typically when you design any system, you can bifurcate into two, one is storage, other is compute.

statement: Requirement: a high response time is acceptable, because performance is not the problem being solved here; the focus is the constraint of not using a traditional database.
detail: Getting performance is a different trick done in past sessions; there are hundreds of known ways to improve it, like caching and batching.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's okay to have high response time because that's not what we are trying to solve over here.

statement: Requirement: the dictionary must be portable; the teacher will point out during the brainstorm whenever a design breaks portability, and its importance becomes clear in the next system and next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what we want is we want portability

statement: The problem statement was deliberately compiled to cover many critical building blocks used day in and day out in the real world.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I just compiled this problem statement in order to cover a lot of critical building blocks

statement: The dictionary is a standard English dictionary (English words and meanings), and serving it is mostly read-only, since a dictionary like Oxford is not updated often.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When you do this, or when you're serving this dictionary, it's mostly read-only.

statement: There are no continuous or live pointed updates: words and meanings are updated weekly (say every Sunday) through a changelog file, received over email, containing the updated words and meanings, which must be applied to the storage engine being built.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Weekly, you will be given a changelog file.

statement: A lookup is always a single word: no autocomplete; given a word, return its meaning; if the word does not exist, return 404.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Given a word, give me the meaning. That's it. If the word does not exist, return 404.

statement: The entire dictionary is one terabyte in size and has 170,000 words in total.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The entire size of the dictionary is one terabyte. And the dictionary in total has 170,000 words.

statement: The brainstorm will cover four axes: storage, query, portability and seamless updates.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: things that we would brainstorm on is around storage query, portability and seamless updates.

statement: A student proposed two ways to store the dictionary: a text file or a JSON file.
detail: The text-file half was taken forward; the JSON half was rejected by the teacher (see the following items). The student himself called one-terabyte JSON 'a bad way to go'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: One is a text file and other is a JSON format basically.

statement: Querying a JSON file requires unmarshaling it, which is a very expensive process, so the student leaned towards a text file.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: and that would be a very expensive process

statement: Storing all data in a single JSON file is a bad fit here: to check whether a word exists you must read the entire JSON file, deserialize it, build an in-memory object (like a hash map) and then check; with a one-terabyte dictionary that is really costly, and the format offers no direct way to access one entry without reading the whole file.
detail: A lot of people put a lot of data in JSON files; the disadvantage is especially bad in this use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is no direct way to access a particular thing in this JSON without reading the entire JSON file, because that's what the format says.

statement: Because a single JSON file cannot be accessed directly, the choice is a simple text file.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which means that what we can pick is we can pick a simple text file.

statement: A student suggested the text file could be like a write-ahead log, with log entries saying a word was updated with a meaning; asked how he was storing it, he moved to a word-equals-meaning, CSV-like format.
detail: The teacher did not take up the log idea; he asked 'How are you storing?' and the discussion continued with the CSV format.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: it will be something like write-ahead log, which will have like, which will create some logs.

statement: The first text-file format is CSV-like: one line per word, e.g. 'apple,fruit' then a new line, then 'Amazon' and its meaning, and so on.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: apple comma fruit and then new line and then let's say you have Amazon
flags: check: speaker boundary - "yeah you can say that" may be one speaker

statement: A student proposed allowing repeated columns/rows with the same word (with updates in mind); the teacher rejected it: there are no columns, only words and meanings, and the dictionary must not contain the same word twice, since people opening the file in any text editor would find it difficult and portability requires no duplicates.
detail: The student said he was thinking of updates and dirty reads; the teacher said he knew where this was going (creating an index on top of it).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, no, no. We don't want same words in the dictionary.
flags: check: speaker boundary unclear around "But that's not now I'm adding"

statement: Added requirement: the dictionary file has no repetitive entries.
detail: The teacher said this one constraint would make things very (sentence unfinished).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let me add it. No repetitive entries.

statement: Asked whether the file would be kept sorted, the student said no: there is no response-time restriction, so sorting is not preferred and words can be in any order.
detail: The teacher accepted the format for starters ('For starters, it is okay'). The design that follows keeps an unsorted file plus an index.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: so I will not prefer sorting here. Okay, so words can come and fit in any order here.
flags: check: speaker of "No, there is no constraint. Will you keep it sorted?" (Teacher?)

statement: When the student jumped to B-trees, the teacher deferred it: it is fun to discover the design step by step, because that solidifies the understanding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's fun to discover it step by step, right? Because that, that solidifies the understanding for him.

statement: A student framed the core requirement: the dictionary must be searchable via key; it is a key-value store where the key is the word and the value is a two- or three-line explanation.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I consider this thing as a key-value store, where key is a word

statement: The dictionary is read-heavy: maybe a thousand-to-one read-to-write ratio, and in fact much more skewed than thousand to one.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: It's much more than thousand to one.
flags: check: speaker of "Much more than that, to be honest. It's much more than thousand to one." (may be the Teacher)

statement: A student required that adding or modifying a word must not 'boil the ocean' (no heavy IO or scanning every file). The teacher agreed a single-word update cannot be very costly, but since updates arrive in a weekly batch, one huge processing pass is acceptable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But given that my total, I'm getting updates in batch, I can still do one huge processing.

statement: A student proposed sorting by key, arguing that without sorting there is no efficient way to search.
detail: The teacher did not rule on sorting directly; he chose a simpler direction (unsorted file plus a one-level index).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If you do not sort it, there is no way you can do a search in a very better way.

statement: A student proposed sharding/partitioning the dictionary into many sorted files and routing a word to the file responsible for it (yesterday's routing pattern), so disk seeks are minimal.
detail: The teacher ruled it out because multiple files kill portability.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Because when you have multiple files, what you are killing is, you are killing portability.

statement: Portability means literally one file, in some format, containing everything needed to read and write it, which can be copied and shipped easily, rather than tens or hundreds of files.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it should be one file which we should be easily able to ship.

statement: A student proposed one zip containing hundreds of folders as the 'single file'.
detail: The teacher rejected it because you would still have to extract it to use it.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, but then you would still have to extract it to use it.
flags: check: speaker of "No, but then you would still have to extract it to use it." (Teacher?)
check: ASR may have garbled "a bit different opinion"

statement: The one-file constraint is not random: its reason becomes clear at the end of the solution, because it forms the foundation for hundreds of systems the teacher will talk about.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because it forms the foundation for hundreds of systems that I'll talk about.

statement: A student proposed logical partitions inside one sorted file, with a header-like section describing which region of the file holds which range of keys; the teacher called it complex enough to touch upon later.
detail: Teacher: multiple partitions within the file with lookups inside them 'is still a complex enough solution that we'll touch upon later'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can have a proper header or something which is a second file which talks about up to this sector

statement: A student suggested encoding records (a key plus a variable-size value) in a format like Parquet instead of JSON or plain lines, accepting some decoding cost; the teacher chose not to digress into Parquet, Avro and similar formats, since not many people know them, and to keep it simple.
detail: Teacher: 'You can use Parquet and whatnot to build it, but instead of going into that complexity, we'll just keep it really simple'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if I use any famous Parquet or any other format, that, that will add a bit of a work there

statement: The teacher deliberately goes in a simpler direction first, so that the base concepts needed to build anything queryable become clear.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm trying to go in a very simpler direction so that the base concepts that we need to build anything queryable works.

statement: Real-world use case: on AWS you can upload any plain CSV file to S3 and still query it seamlessly using a service called Athena.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And we can query it using a service called Athena.

statement: The dictionary exercise simulates that compute engine (S3 with Athena): not at that scale, but how its builders would have thought about and implemented querying simple files; it also has a ton of other applications.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we are trying to build AWS S3, not at that scale, but basically that particular compute engine, how they would have thought of this

statement: A student compared the problem to Lucene: Lucene tokenizes and stores document IDs against keys, and one Lucene index is a single, possibly very large file; here the value is the two- or three-line meaning. The teacher said these were great parts but he is keeping it one level down first.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if you see the Lucene index, they are creating a single file also.

statement: A student proposed binary search, storing offsets as indexes, B+ tree pages, 8 KB blocks and keeping 1000 keys in memory.
detail: The teacher said this over-engineers a very simple word dictionary: no B+ trees, nothing fancy.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We are over engineering.
flags: check: start of sentence may be cut - overlapping speech

statement: Keep the design very simple, because that is where you see the power and the beauty of the system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Keep it very simple, because that's where you see the power of the system.

statement: Naive design: since no traditional DB is allowed, store the dictionary in a simple text file in CSV format: first the key, then the gigantic meaning for that key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's say we store it in a CSV format, but first thing is key, then you have this gigantic meaning for that particular key.

statement: Naive key lookup: open the file, read it line by line until you find the key, stop the iteration, read the meaning and return the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You'll open this file, read this file line by line, find the particular key that you are looking for.

statement: Doing a linear scan for every single read is very expensive, because a dictionary is a very read-heavy application.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now doing this for every single read is very expensive, because dictionary is a very read-heavy application.

statement: With linear search, every read request reads in the worst case the whole one-terabyte file, and on average half a terabyte (0.5 TB = 500 GB) per request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: On an average would be reading half a terabyte for every read

statement: Scanning the file on every read makes things very slow, degrades disk performance, and makes disk sectors go bad from heavy overutilization: hardware problems, software problems and time problems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: third, your disk sectors will go bad because it is very heavily overutilized at the moment

statement: Whenever reads are slow, the only thing that should come to mind for making them faster is indexing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in order to make reads faster, the only thing that should come to your mind is indexing.

statement: Create a small, simple one-level index on top of the data file, to avoid a sequential scan of the entire file when hunting for a key.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Just one level index, simple. What would this index look like?

statement: Each index entry stores the key and its offset in the data file (a student proposed offset and name; the teacher put it as key and offset).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: And the key, right? Key and the offset.

statement: The offset is the byte position of the word's line in the file: the nth byte from the beginning of the file where that line starts (e.g. apple, amazon, book each pointing to their line).
detail: The spoken example numbered the offsets one, two, three (apple, Amazon, book).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And offset is the byte position of that word in that file.
flags: check: speaker boundary - "nth byte ... starts" may complete Student 2's sentence

statement: Read path with a separate index file: open the index file, iterate it line by line until the key (e.g. apple) is found, take its offset, go to the data file, read that entire line, get the meaning and send it to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we went to the corresponding file and then we read this entire line from it, get the meaning and send it to the user.

statement: Scanning the index linearly is still a linear scan, but it is much better than scanning the data: the data scan also wades through the huge meanings, while the index holds only keys and 4-byte offsets, so the small index file is very fast to read sequentially even in the worst case.
detail: The teacher added that when you do file IO you always go in a sequential way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you are not iterating around MBs of data, but rather this is just 4 byte offset.

statement: Before deciding how to read the index, estimate its size with basic computation to see whether it can fit in memory.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Can we fit this index in memory?

statement: A student proposed an index of just 26 entries (A to Z) with their locations.
detail: The teacher corrected that you would still have to go through all the words under that letter, whereas a per-word offset lets you go directly to the line; and since the full index fits in memory, A-to-Z partitioning is unnecessary.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But then still you would have to go to those, those all the words for Apple in order to find that one word.
flags: check: "That's your concern. Right." may be Teacher

statement: The size of each index entry is the length of the key plus the length of the offset.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The size of each entry in the index is how big? The length of the key and the length of the offset.

statement: The average length of a word in the English dictionary is about 4.3 characters, definitely not more than five; the teacher downloaded an entire dictionary and computed it himself.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The length of the word on an average in English dictionary is 4.3 something.

statement: The offset is an integer, which takes 4 bytes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Offset is integer. Integer will take up 4 bytes.

statement: Storing entries one per line adds 2 more characters per entry, one for the comma and one for the new line, so an entry is about 4.3 + 4 + 2 = 10.3 bytes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you add 2 more buffer characters. One for comma and one for new line that you have.

statement: The index size is the number of words (170,000) times the average entry size (10.3 bytes): about 1,751 KB, i.e. roughly 1.75 MB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It will be? 1751 KB, which is equal to 1.751 MB.
flags: check: the student's product is heard as "17,000,000" bytes, which does not match 1751 KB (170,000 x 10.3 = 1,751,000)

statement: An index of 1.75 MB fits in RAM very easily; it is 'peanuts' even though the data file is one terabyte.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: 1.751, you can fit it in RAM very easily.

statement: Number crunching is very important when designing any system: what looks huge (a one-terabyte file, 170,000 words) turned out to need an index of only 1.75 MB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is why number crunching is very important when you are designing any system.

statement: Keep the index stored on disk and load it into an in-memory hash map when the API server starts; on a request, check the hash map for the word, get the offset, go to the data file, read the line from that offset and return the meaning.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's like create a hash map out of this in memory, given a word, check the hash map, get the offset, go to this file

statement: One simple number crunch made the system much better: instead of over-complicating things, keep it very simple with one level of indexing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of over complicating things we just keep it very simple, that one level of indexing.

statement: With the in-memory index there is no linear scan: each lookup is a direct pointed read on the data file at the offset given by the index, which makes reads much faster. This settles the storage and querying side.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We are directly doing a pointed read on this file with the help of this index.

statement: The design now has two files, an index file and a data file (data.dictionary); shipping the dictionary as two files breaks portability, so it must become one file.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This breaks the portability thing. We want this to be just one file.

statement: A student proposed not persisting the index at all and building it in memory on every startup.
detail: The teacher rejected it because every startup would have to iterate through the entire data file, which is avoidable since the file changes only once a week.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So which means on every startup you have to iterate through this entire
flags: check: sentence cut off, 3 s pause follows

statement: Merge the two files into one: concatenate the index and the data into one gigantic file. This raises a new challenge: how does the reader know where the index ends and the data begins?
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So now you are merging this two file into one gigantic file in which you have index.

statement: A student proposed marking the boundary between index and data with a special line or separator.
detail: The teacher later replaced the separator idea with storing the byte offset (index size) at the start of the file, which removes the need for a separator.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: There has to be some line or some, some special information.

statement: A student proposed pre-allocating a fixed-size region for the index (e.g. the first 2 MB, more than today's 1.751 MB, since few new words get added), so the reader knows the first 2 MB are the index.
detail: The teacher called it a good approach and a very nice hack, but it wastes some space, and asked to be more frugal.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: That's a good approach. That's a very nice hack, but it's not space.

statement: A student proposed writing data from the top of the file downwards and the index from the bottom upwards like a stack.
detail: The teacher asked how you would know where one ends and the other begins once they are next to each other, and noted the gap between them is unused space; the student fell back to a separator.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But the day when these two are right next to each other, how would you know when one finished and other begins?
flags: check: "So then you are wasting this much of space ... but someday" may be the teacher

statement: The reader must know where to stop reading the index: if index and data are both CSV lines read one by one into the hash table, the reader would also load data lines as entries (e.g. replace apple's offset entry with 'fruit').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need to know when to stop.
flags: check: possible ASR loop - teacher may be counting entries

statement: A student proposed reserving a specific position at the very start of the file to store the boundary information, updated as data is added; the teacher found it interesting and refined it.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can choose a specific index to store that information.

statement: Instead of storing a separator, store the byte offset directly at the start of the file; this eradicates the need for a separator, and on load the reader first reads this first chunk to know where the data begins.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Instead of storing the separator, can you not directly store the byte offset?

statement: A header is the classic mechanism of every file format (PNG, JPG, MP3, AVI): the first few bytes contain meta information about everything else in the file, and what they hold depends on the format, as specified by its creator.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And this is a classic way of having a header in any file format of the world.

statement: Because a single file contains multiple sections, the header stores the information about each of the sections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because it contains multiple sections, you are storing the information about each of the sections in this header.

statement: The header has to be of fixed size; it cannot go beyond that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And now this has to be a fixed size header.

statement: Header field 1: the first 8 bytes hold a name (e.g. O-U-R-D-I-C-T) that tells the decoder this is our dictionary file.
case_study: Dictionary file header field: format name.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So the first 8 bytes will denote that this is our dictionary.

statement: In the PNG format, the first bytes (said as the first 3 bytes, P-N-N-G) tell the decoder it is a PNG file; MP3 has some other bytes, and so on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So in the PNG format, the first 3 bytes is P-N-N-G.

statement: If the teacher built his own database called AODB ("Arpit's outstanding database"), its first four bytes would say AODB, and his decoder would recognise an AODB file and know what components it holds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say I build my own database, to call it AODB, Arpit's outstanding database, for some reason.

statement: Header field 2: a version number (a 4-byte integer), since a file may have multiple variants, e.g. version 1 stores index first then data, version 2 data first then index; the decoder acts according to the version.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Maybe in version two, you have data first and then index.

statement: Header field 3: the index size (4 bytes), i.e. how big the index is, e.g. the integer for 1.75 MB; alternatively a start offset of the data could be stored.
case_study: Dictionary file header field: index size.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The next four bytes is index size.

statement: The dictionary header is a fixed-width 16 bytes: 8 bytes name + 4 bytes version + 4 bytes index size.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So this is the header that you just added, which is 16 bytes.

statement: On boot, the application server reads the first 16 bytes of the file as the header: the first 8 bytes say it is our dictionary, the next 4 are the version and the next 4 the index size; it then reads that many bytes as the index and builds a hash table from it, and everything after that is data, which the index offsets point into.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So it would read the first 16 bytes, out of which it would find the first 8 bytes and understood it is our dictionary.

statement: This makes the whole dictionary shippable, and it is the classic way to build any custom file format: divide the file into compartments (here index and data) and keep a header that tells where each compartment lies.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is literally creating compartments in the file that you have, and having a header that tells you where which compartment lies.

statement: Other formats use sections too: in JPG there are different frames; in MP4 the header says where the video part and the audio part are, the video has first, second, third frames and the audio part holds waveform information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In case of MP4, it would be where is the video part? Where is the audio part?

statement: A single file with a header can be shipped easily across systems or to end users, and anyone who has the decoder can read it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Anyone having this decoder can read this file

statement: Parquet, which comes up in data engineering, also has headers and information.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Parquet format also has some headers and information, right?

statement: JSON has no header: a JSON file is a simple text file, so you must read the entire file and have the JSON decoder parse the curly braces, quotes and strings into an in-memory dictionary before getting any information out of it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because it doesn't have header, you have to read the entire file to get the information out of it.

statement: CSV in general does not have a header, whereas formats like PPT and PDF have one; you can also define your own custom format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CSV in general does not have a header, right?

statement: The teacher once tried to write his own image format, which is how he learned how file formats and headers work.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I tried to write my own image format.

statement: Every file format has its own encoder and decoder: the encoder creates the file in that specific format and the decoder decodes it; this holds for image, video, audio, any format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So encoder creates that file in that specific format and decoder decodes it.

statement: The early-internet browser error 'this web browser does not support TIF format' means the browser has no decoder for that format: given that set of bytes, it does not know how to interpret them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this web browser does not support TIF format.

statement: Our decoder's logic: the first 16 bytes are the header, which gives the index size, from which the index and then the data are located; offsets in the index point into the data part. This holds for every file format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it would know for 16 bytes is header, through which I would get the size of the index, and from which I'll get the data.

statement: Because of the portability constraint, the dictionary became a single file instead of multiple shipped files.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because of that one constraint that I added, portability, you see that how we were able to create this as just one file

statement: Recap and transition: so far file formats, portability, headers and indexing for faster reads; next comes the infrastructure side, i.e. how to serve actual user requests, starting with a seed design to improve on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now we'll touch upon infrastructure side of things.

statement: Serving architecture: a request from the end user comes to a load balancer, behind which a bunch of API servers serve the incoming requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Behind the load balancer, we have bunch of API servers whose job is to serve the incoming requests that are there.

statement: The API exposes a GET endpoint on /word that returns the word's meaning; the load balancer forwards each request to one of the API server instances.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So slash word is we are exposing and we are doing a GET on it and we get the meaning around it.

statement: A student proposed a shared disk storage that all API servers query to get the file.
detail: After probing why not keep a copy on every server, the teacher concluded on a central place to store the dictionary, crediting this proposal.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So can we have a shared disk storage for all the API servers that they can query to get the file?

statement: Asked why not store the file on every API server, a student said updates would be tedious (each server must be updated and some may be unavailable).
detail: The teacher countered that updates are not real time but one bulk update every Sunday, so this is not really a problem.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: But updates are not real time. Updates are weekly. Is that still a problem?

statement: A student raised that a partially failed update would leave data inconsistent across servers.
detail: The teacher called it a valid point but not a real problem yet, since meanings do not change dramatically (apple 'a fruit' vs a slightly reworded meaning is not the end of the world).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You may have inconsistency in data in case your update partially fails, but it's a meaning.

statement: When proposing a solution, you should have thought in depth about the disadvantages of the alternatives.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you should have thought of disadvantages of other part in depth, which is what I'm trying to prove.

statement: The biggest pain of storing the same dictionary file on every server is cost: duplicated storage across many servers. Inconsistency and tedious updates are acceptable; cost is not.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Biggest pain, cost.

statement: Real-world system design is about doing the bare minimum things at the bare minimum cost; if you are not thinking about cost you are not building good systems, and whether a solution is cost-efficient should be the first thing that comes to mind.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A real world system design is all about doing things, doing the bare minimum things at the bare minimum cost. Always remember this.

statement: Anything can be made faster by throwing money at a cloud provider: with one terabyte of RAM on each machine you could load the whole dictionary into one in-memory hash table with no index at all, but that is not a good solution because it is not cost effective.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If I can have one terabyte RAM over here on each of this machine, I can just load the entire dictionary in memory.

statement: Duplicating the dictionary on each server's disk (SSDs, which are very costly) means that with 100 servers you hold 100 terabytes of redundant data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have 100 servers, so you are having 100 terabytes of redundant data.

statement: Therefore do not store the file on each server; keep the dictionary in one central place.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: have a central place where you are storing the dictionary.

statement: A student proposed storing the single dictionary file on Amazon S3, because it is very cheap and optimized for blob storage.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So can we use something like Amazon S3 in this case to store this file?

statement: S3's get-object call accepts parameters for the bytes to read, so one can fetch just the header/index bytes (the index size is known), take a word's offset, and fetch just that byte range to answer the user.
detail: The teacher responded 'Great, great, great' and called it something very interesting.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: get object has some query params where we can actually pass the bytes that we want to read.

statement: First pin down the core properties you want from the system, then pick a particular technology.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We still want to know what are the core properties we want from the system. And then we would pick a particular technology, right?

statement: Shared storage is wanted because replicating the data to every server is cost-inefficient; what is common across multiple servers is the network, so the dictionary needs a common place accessible over the network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what is common across multiple servers? Network, which means you need a common place which is accessible over network.

statement: A common place accessible over the network is any block storage or a database; databases are ruled out, so the gigantic file goes on block storage such as S3, which keeps portability because it is still one file.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We are still not giving up our portability. We still have this one file on S3.

statement: The design assumed a normal disk: read the header bytes to learn the index size, read the whole index to build an in-memory hash table, then do random reads in the data section; whatever storage replaces the disk must support this.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We're reading this entire thing to build an in-memory hash table and then doing random reads on this data section.

statement: The generic term for what is needed is network attached storage: storage accessible over the network that gives file system semantics.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So generic term for this is a network attached storage.

statement: The bare-minimum feature required is random reads: being able to say 'from this file, at this offset, read n bytes', just as a normal disk lets you seek to a location and read that many bytes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It means that I could provide a thing that say that from this file at this offset read n bytes.

statement: S3 gives file-system-level semantics, so it can also be used as a distributed file system: you do not have to read the entire file, you can ask for a given number of bytes at a given offset and get exactly those bytes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: S3 gives you all the file system level semantics because of which it can be used as a distributed file system as well.

statement: S3 is not special: it can be replaced by any network attached storage with the same semantics, e.g. HDFS, or literal physical network hard disks in a data center (Dell network hard disks are famous); S3 is used only because everyone understands it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's not that I prefer S3. It's just that you can replace S3 with any network attached storage.

statement: Each API server needs to know the dictionary's file path on S3, which can be passed as static configuration; the teacher will go deeper into this because deployment is still to be discussed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What each API server need to know is needs to know the file path on S3.

statement: API server boot flow on S3: from the configured path, read the first 16 bytes and interpret them as the header (dictionary file, index size); make another S3 call to read that many bytes of index and build an in-memory hash table; then start serving requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: then it would make another S3 call to read those many bytes and create a hash table, in-memory hash table over here.

statement: GET flow: the request reaches any API server, which checks its in-memory hash table; if the word is absent it returns 404; if present it takes the offset and does a random read on the S3 file at that offset for that many bytes, which the S3 API supports (as do HDFS and network hard disks).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If the word exists, good enough. If it does not exist, 404, right?

statement: Each read fetches only the bytes of interest, nothing before and nothing after: the bare minimum.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you can seamlessly read the bytes that you are interested in and nothing before that, nothing after that.

statement: The beauty of the system: it achieves efficient pointed reads of a single record from S3 without reading the entire file, which effectively builds a database, since a database is a key-value store; this is a key-value store supporting a huge amount of gets on S3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We just build a key-value store that supports huge amount of gets on S3.

statement: The ability to fire pointed queries on S3 without reading the entire file is 'magical' and has a ton of applications.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So we got this ability to fire pointed queries on S3 without us having to read this entire file. And that is magical.

statement: Later the teacher will talk about how to extend this pointed-read capability into building various applications.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We'll talk about how to extend this part into building various applications out of it.
